title: Four Return Measures and What Each One Hides
summary: The internal rate of return measures speed, the equity multiple measures size, and cash-on-cash measures annual income to equity, each levered or unlevered. Read alone, each can mislead, especially on short holds and early distributions, and every quoted return is pre-tax until tax and fees are taken out.
body:
No single number tells you whether a deal is good. The internal rate of return measures speed, the equity multiple measures size, cash-on-cash measures what you receive along the way, and every one of them is a pre-tax promise until the tax and fees are taken out. Read all four together or be fooled by one.

Recall

Q. Last week, REGA covered the rules that cap rent and raise costs. Why does rent regulation belong in the base case of a pro forma?

A. Because revenue can only be underwritten from rents you can legally charge. Anything that depends on a change in law or tenancy is upside, not base case.

Q. In Week 13, Sage set out sources and uses. What must be true of the two sides?

A. They must balance: every dollar of cost must have a named source, and the equity must be in before the debt is drawn if the lender requires it.

Q. In Week 7, Warrick built your personal balance sheet. What is liquid net worth?

A. Net worth after removing assets that cannot be turned into cash quickly without a large discount, such as your share of a project or real estate.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Sage here, with Elias joining for the tax. Every investor, partner and lender you meet will describe a deal by its returns. Brokers lead with the IRR because it is usually the most flattering. Investors are paid on returns, and promotes, the developer's share of profit above a hurdle, are often triggered by them. If you can see what each return measure hides, you will avoid deals that only look good, and you will present your own deals in a way experienced investors trust.

The internal rate of return measures speed

In plain English, the internal rate of return, or IRR, is the annual growth rate at which the money you put in becomes the money you get back. Last week Nadia taught net present value. The IRR is the discount rate at which net present value is exactly zero.

The professional framing: IRR accounts for timing, which is its strength. It rewards getting money back early. That is also its weakness. It says nothing about how much money you made, only how fast it grew. A small profit returned quickly can show a higher IRR than a large profit returned slowly.

First worked example, hypothetical round numbers. Deal A turns $100 into $200 over ten years. Deal B turns $100 into $130 over two years. Deal A's IRR is about 7.2 percent a year, because $100 growing at 7.2 percent for ten years is about $200. Deal B's IRR is about 14 percent a year. Deal B looks twice as good on IRR. But Deal A doubled your money, and Deal B left you with $130 and the problem of finding another deal for your capital after two years.

The equity multiple measures size

The equity multiple is total cash returned to equity divided by total equity invested. Deal A's multiple is 2.0 times; Deal B's is 1.3 times. It measures how much wealth the deal created, and ignores how long it took. Read alone it is as misleading as IRR: a 2.0 times multiple over thirty years is a poor result.

So professionals quote the two together, always. "A 14 percent IRR and a 1.3 times multiple over two years" tells a reader almost everything. "A 14 percent IRR" alone tells them very little.

Say that out loud now. IRR is speed. The multiple is size. Never quote one without the other and the hold period.

Cash-on-cash measures what arrives along the way

Cash-on-cash return is one year's cash distributed to equity divided by the equity invested. Second worked example, hypothetical. You and your investors put $4,000,000 of equity into a $10,000,000 stabilised building. After paying the loan, the building distributes $400,000 in its first year. Cash-on-cash is 10 percent. It tells an income-focused investor what they can live on, and it ignores the sale entirely, so a building with a weak cash yield and a large expected gain on sale will look poor on this measure and strong on IRR. Neither view is wrong; they answer different questions.

Unlevered and levered

Each measure can be calculated two ways. Unlevered returns treat the project as if it were bought with all equity, so they measure the property itself. Levered returns include the loan, so they measure what equity actually receives after debt service and loan repayment. Leverage usually raises the levered IRR when the property's return exceeds the cost of debt, and it always raises the risk. Roman shows you the arithmetic on Day 3. The habit to form now: when someone quotes an IRR, ask whether it is levered or unlevered, and what loan it assumes.

The four IRR traps

  1. The short-hold trap. A quick exit inflates IRR while the multiple stays small. Ask for the multiple.
  2. The early-distribution trap. Refinancing early and returning capital raises IRR sharply, because money came back sooner, even though the project's risk often rises. Day 2 takes a case apart.
  3. The reinvestment trap. IRR quietly implies that every distribution can be redeployed at a similar return. If you cannot find another deal like it, your real wealth grows more slowly than the IRR suggests.
  4. The scale trap. A 30 percent IRR on $100,000 creates less wealth than a 12 percent IRR on $5,000,000. Ask for dollar profit.

After-tax leakage

Elias here. Every return above is usually quoted before tax, and often before fees. Between the property and the investor's pocket, money leaks: tax on income at the entity or investor level, tax on the gain at sale, the recapture of earlier tax depreciation, withholding tax when money crosses a border, and asset management, acquisition and disposition fees. Two investors in the same deal can earn very different after-tax returns depending on where they are taxed and how they hold their interest. Treat any return as pre-tax unless it says otherwise, and ask for the after-tax version that applies to you. I will not give rates here; the specific rules must be verified against the primary source and with your tax adviser.

How the best do it

Disciplined institutional investors tend to set hurdles on more than one measure at once: a minimum IRR and a minimum equity multiple, with promotes to the developer paid only when both are met. That single design choice defeats the short-hold and early-distribution traps, because a quick, small win does not clear the multiple hurdle. A small developer can copy it directly when negotiating a joint venture, and can underwrite his own deals the same way.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing deals, or structuring a promote, around IRR alone, which rewards speed over wealth and can encourage early refinancing that weakens the project. The control: every deal summary you read or write shows levered and unlevered IRR, equity multiple, dollar profit, hold period, peak equity and an after-tax figure for the investor in question.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner compares two deals by IRR. The second beginner's mistake is to compare a levered IRR from one sponsor with an unlevered IRR from another and think they are measuring the same thing.

Callback

In Week 7, Warrick asked you to define "enough" and to watch concentration. Returns are where that question becomes practical. A high IRR on a small slice tells you little about your wealth; a moderate IRR on a large, concentrated position can decide your whole balance sheet. Ask what each deal does to your liquid net worth and your concentration, not just what rate it earns.

Recap

IRR measures speed, the equity multiple measures size, cash-on-cash measures annual income to equity, and each can be levered or unlevered. Quote IRR with the multiple and the hold period, beware short holds, early distributions, reinvestment and scale, and treat every return as pre-tax until tax and fees are removed.

Next: Ford, with Roman assisting, on a composite case where an early refinance made the IRR and broke the project.
checklist: Quote IRR only with the equity multiple and the hold period.
Ask whether every IRR is levered or unlevered, and what loan it assumes.
Ask for dollar profit and peak equity beside any percentage return.
Check for short holds and early distributions that inflate IRR.
Treat every return as pre-tax and pre-fee unless stated otherwise.
Ask for the after-tax return that applies to your own position.
Set hurdles on both IRR and equity multiple in any promote you negotiate.
head: Field checklist
speak: No single return tells me whether a deal is good. The internal rate of return measures speed: the annual rate at which money in grows into money out. The equity multiple measures size: total cash back divided by cash in. Cash-on-cash measures one year's distribution against equity. Turning 100 dollars into 200 over ten years is a 2 times multiple but only about a 7 percent IRR; turning 100 into 130 over two years is a 14 percent IRR but only 1.3 times. So I always quote IRR with the multiple and the hold period, and I ask whether it is levered or unlevered. I watch four traps: short holds, early distributions, the reinvestment assumption and scale. And every quoted return is before tax and fees, so I ask for the after-tax figure that applies to me. In a promote, I set hurdles on both IRR and multiple.
terms: Internal rate of return (IRR) — the annual discount rate at which the net present value of a deal's cash flows is exactly zero; a measure of how fast invested money grows.
Equity multiple — total cash returned to equity divided by total equity invested; a measure of how much wealth a deal created, regardless of time.
Cash-on-cash return — one year's cash distributed to equity divided by the equity invested.

hostile.q: Your deal shows a 22 percent IRR. Why should I believe it is a good deal?
hostile.a: You shouldn't from the IRR alone. Here it is beside the rest: a 1.4 times equity multiple over two and a half years, dollar profit, peak equity, and the unlevered IRR of about 10 percent, which tells you how much of the 22 comes from the property and how much from leverage. The after-tax return depends on how you hold your interest, and your adviser should run that. If the multiple were below 1.3, I would not offer the deal at all, whatever the IRR.

title: The Refinance That Made the IRR
summary: This is a composite example: an early, maximum refinance returned most of the equity, lifted the IRR and paid the developer's promote. When rates rose, the larger floating-rate loan failed its coverage covenant and the developer's guarantee was called. The lesson is that a speed measure set the financing and the pay.
body:
This is a composite example: a developer refinanced a newly finished building early, returned most of the equity, and posted an IRR investors celebrated. Two years later the larger loan failed its coverage test, and the guarantee was called. The IRR was real; the wealth it described was not.

Recall

Q. Last week, Sage reverse engineered rent and lease-up. Why work backward from the loan maturity?

A. To find the lease-up pace needed to reach stabilised NOI, and so the permanent loan, before the construction loan matures.

Q. In Week 13, Ford took apart Holyrood. What was its rule?

A. No estimate leaves my hands, in writing or out loud, without its class, its date, its scope basis and its contingency stated alongside it.

Q. In Week 7, Ford took apart Olympia and York. What was its lesson about wealth?

A. That real wealth concentrated in a few giant projects and funded with short-term money could not wait out a downturn; it was illiquid when it needed to be liquid.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Ford here, with Roman on the finance. This is a composite example, built from a pattern common in leveraged real estate rather than from one named company. I use a composite because the pattern matters more than any single set of facts, and I will not invent figures and attach them to a real firm. The pattern: a return measure that rewards speed, a promote triggered by it, and a refinance that looked like success. All numbers are hypothetical.

Step 1: Timeline

Year 0: a developer and three investors fund a $20,000,000 rental project with $6,000,000 of equity and a $14,000,000 construction loan. Year 2: the building completes and leases up quickly. Year 2.5: values are high and credit is cheap, so the developer refinances with a $19,000,000 floating-rate loan, repays the construction loan, and distributes about $5,000,000 to the investors. The deal's IRR jumps, the developer's promote is earned and paid, and the investor report celebrates. Year 4: interest rates rise sharply, NOI stays flat as new supply arrives, and the loan's coverage ratio falls below its covenant. Year 4.5: the lender declares a default, and a recourse guarantee the developer gave on the refinance is called.

Step 2: Key decisions

Three decisions. Refinancing to the maximum loan the appraisal would support, rather than a loan sized to survive a downside. Taking floating-rate debt without a hedge to make the larger loan affordable on paper. And agreeing a promote calculated on IRR alone, payable on the refinance, so the developer was paid in full before the deal had proved itself.

Step 3: Assumptions

The deal assumed rates would stay near where they were, rents would keep rising, and the building could be sold or refinanced again before the new loan matured. Each was plausible in year 2.5. None was tested in a severe case. The appraisal behind the refinance valued the building at a cap rate near the low of the cycle, and nobody asked what the loan looked like at a cap rate one point higher.

Step 4: Incentives

The developer's promote was triggered by IRR, and IRR rewards early cash. Investors liked receiving most of their money back quickly. The lender earned fees on a larger loan. Every incentive in the chain pointed toward the refinance, and none rewarded keeping the leverage modest. Week 3's principal-agent problem, written into a joint venture agreement.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The refinance loan's coverage ratio at closing was close to the covenant level, leaving almost no room for rate rises. The equity multiple at the refinance was still only about 0.8 times returned, so most of the deal's wealth was still a promise. New supply was visible in the area's permit data. And the developer gave a recourse guarantee to get the larger loan, turning a project risk into a personal one.

Say that out loud now. An early refinance raises the IRR and the risk at the same time.

Step 6: Point of no return

The point of no return was the distribution. Once $5,000,000 had left the project and the promote had been paid, the building carried a loan sized for a good year with no cash cushion behind it. When rates rose, there was no reserve to pay down the loan, and the investors who had received their money back had no wish to put it in again.

Step 7: Root cause

Roman's reading: the root cause was letting a speed measure, IRR, set the financing and the compensation, so that taking cash out early was rewarded and keeping the project resilient was not. The returns were calculated correctly. The decision was optimised for the measure instead of for the wealth.

The numbers that would have warned them

Hypothetical. On the refinance, NOI was $1,300,000. At an interest rate of 5 percent, interest-only, the $19,000,000 loan cost $950,000 a year, a coverage ratio of about 1.37. At 6.5 percent it would cost $1,235,000, a ratio of about 1.05, below a typical covenant. A one-and-a-half point rise in rates, not an unusual move over a few years, was enough. That calculation took two lines and was not done.

A second applied example, on the investor's side. An investor offered a share of a refinance distribution should ask two questions before celebrating. What is my multiple so far, including this distribution? And if the project defaults after I am repaid, could any of this distribution be clawed back, under the agreement or under the law on payments made while a company was in trouble? The second is a legal question for a lawyer; Week 89 covers voidable transfers as a concept.

What a careful sponsor would have done

The same building, the same year 2.5, a different decision. Size the new loan so that coverage stays at or above the covenant with rates 2 points higher and the cap rate 1 point higher. Hypothetical: at 7 percent, a loan with coverage of 1.25 on $1,300,000 of NOI can cost no more than $1,040,000 a year, which supports about $14,900,000 interest-only. Refinance to that, hedge the rate or fix it, and distribute what is left after repaying the construction loan and leaving a reserve: well under $1,000,000 instead of $5,000,000. The IRR is lower in the investor report. The promote, measured on multiple as well as IRR, waits for the sale. And when rates rise, the building passes its covenant, the guarantee is never called, and the investors are paid at exit from a project that survived. Slower on the scoreboard, far richer in the end.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that a promote or a performance target tied to IRR alone pays people to weaken the project. The control: hurdles on both IRR and equity multiple, promotes paid on realised cash after the downside case is still covered, and any refinance distribution sized so the new loan survives a rate and cap rate stress.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner sees money returned early as risk removed. Often it is risk added: the same building now carries more debt and less equity.

Callback

In Week 10, Rule 10 said never borrow against income that does not yet exist. A maximum refinance at a cycle-low cap rate is a close cousin: it borrows against a value that exists only while rates stay low. Both rules ask the same question, can the deal survive losing the assumption it is built on?

Recap

A composite: an early, maximum refinance returned equity, inflated the IRR and paid the promote, and when rates rose the larger loan failed its covenant and the developer's guarantee was called. Rule 15: I never accept an IRR without its equity multiple, dollar profit, hold period and after-tax figure beside it, and I never take a distribution that leaves the project unable to survive its downside case.

Next: Roman on how leverage raises the return and the risk together.
checklist: Size any refinance to survive a rate rise and a higher cap rate, not to the maximum appraisal supports.
Test the coverage ratio at the current rate plus 1.5 points before refinancing.
Check the equity multiple, not just IRR, at any distribution.
Set promote hurdles on both IRR and equity multiple.
Pay promotes on realised cash after the downside case is still covered.
Hedge or stress floating-rate debt before relying on it.
Ask a lawyer whether a distribution could be clawed back if the project later fails.
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite case. A developer finished a 20 million dollar building, leased it fast, and at a cycle-low cap rate refinanced with a bigger floating-rate loan, returning about 5 million to investors. The IRR jumped and the developer's promote, tied to IRR alone, was paid. Two years later rates rose, NOI stayed flat, the coverage ratio fell below its covenant, and the guarantee the developer gave on the refinance was called. The returns were calculated correctly; the decisions were optimised for the measure, not for the wealth. Two lines of arithmetic would have warned them: at 5 percent the loan covered 1.37 times, at 6.5 percent only about 1.05. My rule: I never accept an IRR without its multiple, profit, hold period and after-tax figure, and I never take a distribution that leaves the project unable to survive its downside case.
terms: Promote — the developer's share of profits above an agreed hurdle, sometimes called carried interest.
Cash-out refinance — replacing a loan with a larger one and distributing the difference to owners.
Recourse guarantee — a personal promise to repay some or all of a loan if the borrower cannot, putting the guarantor's own assets at risk.

hostile.q: Values are up. Why won't you refinance to the maximum and return our capital now?
hostile.a: Because the maximum loan only works while rates and cap rates stay where they are today. At today's rate the larger loan covers about 1.37 times; one and a half points higher it falls near 1.05, below the covenant. I will refinance to a loan that survives that stress and distribute what that allows. You get capital back, the project keeps a cushion, and the promote is calculated on multiple as well as IRR, so neither of us is paid for taking that risk.

rule: Rule 15: I never accept an IRR without its equity multiple, dollar profit, hold period and after-tax figure beside it, and I never take a distribution that leaves the project unable to survive its downside case.

title: Leverage Raises the Return and the Risk Together
summary: Leverage is positive when the property earns more than the debt costs and negative when it does not. It magnifies gains and losses on equity by roughly one over the equity share, and the loan terms decide how far income can fall before the building cannot pay. The Wealth Ledger counts guarantees as personal leverage.
body:
Borrowing raises the return on your equity only while the property earns more than the debt costs, and it raises the risk to your equity every time. Leverage does not create value; it moves the property's result, good or bad, onto a smaller pile of your money.

Recall

Q. In Week 14, the lender's appraiser put market rent 100 dollars below yours. What settles that disagreement best?

A. Evidence: signed leases and comparable rents that support your figure, offered calmly, rather than argument or pressure on the appraiser.

Q. In Week 13, Priya called finance costs the line that grows while you wait. Why is construction interest circular?

A. Because interest is charged on the loan, and the loan has to be large enough to pay the interest, so each estimate changes the other until they settle.

Q. In Week 7, Warrick priced the liquidity floor. What does holding it cost, and what does its absence cost?

A. Holding it costs the return the cash could have earned in a deal. Not holding it can cost a forced sale or an unmet guarantee, which is far more.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman here. Sage told you on Day 1 to ask whether any IRR is levered or unlevered. Today you see why that question matters. Almost every developer uses debt. Used well, it lets a small amount of equity control a large project and earn a high return. Used badly, it is the single most common way developers lose everything. The arithmetic is simple enough to do in your head, and you should do it before every loan you sign.

Positive and negative leverage

In plain English, leverage is positive when the property earns more on each dollar than the loan charges for it. The equity keeps the difference, so its return goes up. Leverage is negative when the loan costs more than the property earns. The equity has to make up the difference, so its return goes down.

First worked example, hypothetical round numbers. A stabilised building costs $10,000,000 and earns NOI of $600,000. Unlevered, its cash yield is 6 percent. Now borrow $6,000,000 interest-only at 5 percent: $300,000 a year. Equity is $4,000,000. Cash left for equity after interest is $600,000 minus $300,000, which is $300,000. Cash-on-cash return is $300,000 divided by $4,000,000, 7.5 percent. Borrowing at 5 percent against a 6 percent property raised the equity's cash return from 6 to 7.5 percent. That is positive leverage.

Same building, but the loan costs 7 percent: $420,000 a year. Cash left for equity is $180,000. Cash-on-cash is $180,000 divided by $4,000,000, 4.5 percent. Borrowing at 7 percent against a 6 percent property cut the equity's cash return below what it would earn with no loan at all. That is negative leverage, and when interest rates rise above property yields, it is what most leveraged owners experience.

The professional framing: compare the property's unlevered return with the all-in cost of the debt. For cash yield, compare the cap rate or yield on cost with the loan's constant, which is annual debt service, interest plus principal, divided by the loan amount. For total return, compare the unlevered IRR with the debt cost. Leverage helps only on the side of that line where the property wins.

Say that out loud now. Leverage is positive only while the property earns more than the debt costs.

Leverage magnifies losses exactly as it magnifies gains

Second worked example, hypothetical. Keep the $10,000,000 building, $6,000,000 loan and $4,000,000 of equity. If the building's value rises 10 percent, to $11,000,000, and you sell, equity receives $5,000,000 after repaying the loan: a 25 percent gain on $4,000,000, from a 10 percent gain in the property. If the value falls 10 percent, to $9,000,000, equity receives $3,000,000: a 25 percent loss from a 10 percent fall. At a $9,000,000 loan instead of $6,000,000, the same 10 percent fall would wipe out the equity entirely.

The ratio of the change in equity to the change in the property is roughly one divided by the equity share. With 40 percent equity, each move in the property is magnified about two and a half times on the equity. With 10 percent equity, about ten times. Week 10 showed the same effect through a cap rate move; this is the same effect through the sale price.

What leverage does to IRR

On Day 5, Sage will work a full example. The headline is that with debt cheaper than the property's return, levered IRR can be far higher than unlevered IRR, in Sage's example about 16 percent levered against about 9 percent unlevered. With debt at 7 percent on the same property, the levered IRR falls to about 13 percent, three points lower, while the risk to equity is just as high. Ask, every time: how much of this return is the property, and how much is the loan?

Remember that the cost of debt is not fixed unless you fix it. On a floating-rate loan, the line between positive and negative leverage moves every time the benchmark rate moves, so a deal that is comfortably positive at signing can turn negative during the hold without anything changing at the building. That is why the composite case on Day 2 failed: the property did not get worse; the loan got more expensive. When you compare the property's return with the debt cost, use the rate you could face, not only the rate you are offered today.

The coverage cushion

Leverage also sets how far income can fall before the loan is in trouble. In the first example, NOI is $600,000 and interest is $300,000, a coverage ratio of 2.0. NOI could halve before the building failed to pay its interest. At 7 percent, coverage is about 1.43, and a fall in NOI of about 30 percent leaves the building unable to cover it. Same building, same tenants; the loan terms alone decide how much bad news the equity can absorb.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for your personal balance sheet. Leverage on a project does not stay at the project if you have guaranteed the loan. A personal guarantee adds the project's debt to your personal risk, even though it does not appear as a liability on your balance sheet until it is called. Keep two numbers beside every project on your personal statement: your equity at cost, and the maximum amount your guarantee could require. Then add up the second column across all projects and compare it with your liquid net worth and your liquidity floor. If one bad year in two projects at once could exceed your liquid net worth, you are more leveraged personally than any single loan suggests. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financial decision.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is borrowing as much as a lender will offer because the levered IRR looks better, when the property's return is close to or below the cost of debt. The control: before every loan, compare the property's unlevered return with the loan constant and the debt cost, calculate coverage at today's rate and at two points higher, and size the loan to survive the higher case.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner believes leverage always raises returns. It raises them only while the property out-earns the debt, and it raises the risk regardless.

Callback

In Week 7, Rule 7 said never let one project, or one lender's change of mind, be able to take everything. Leverage is the dial that decides whether a single bad year can do that. Low leverage gives you time; high leverage gives you a deadline.

Recap

Leverage is positive when the property earns more than the debt costs and negative when it does not. It magnifies equity gains and losses by roughly one over the equity share. It can lift IRR sharply when debt is cheap and barely at all when it is not, and it sets the cushion before the loan is in trouble. Guarantees bring project leverage onto your personal balance sheet.

Next: Elias on where tax leaks out of a return.
checklist: Compare the property's unlevered return with the loan constant and the debt cost before borrowing.
Calculate cash-on-cash with and without the loan.
Show equity gain and loss for a 10 percent rise and fall in value.
Calculate coverage at today's rate and two points higher.
Ask how much of any levered IRR comes from the property and how much from the loan.
Size the loan to survive the higher-rate case.
Total the maximum guarantee exposure across all projects against your liquid net worth.
head: Field checklist
speak: Leverage moves the property's result onto a smaller pile of my money. If a 10 million dollar building earns 6 percent and I borrow 6 million at 5 percent, my 4 million of equity earns 7.5 percent cash-on-cash. That is positive leverage. If the loan costs 7 percent, my equity earns 4.5 percent, less than with no loan at all. That is negative leverage. Leverage magnifies losses as much as gains: with 40 percent equity, a 10 percent fall in value is a 25 percent loss to me. The loan terms also set the cushion: at 5 percent interest covers 2 times, so income could halve; at 7 percent, a 30 percent fall breaks it. So before every loan I compare the property's return with the cost of debt, test coverage two points higher, and size the loan to survive that. And I count every guarantee as my own leverage.
terms: Positive leverage — when the property earns more than the debt costs, so borrowing raises the return on equity.
Negative leverage — when the debt costs more than the property earns, so borrowing lowers the return on equity.
Loan constant — annual debt service, interest plus principal, divided by the loan amount; compared with the property's yield to test leverage.

hostile.q: Your levered IRR is 16 percent. How much of that is the building?
hostile.a: About 9 percent. That is the unlevered IRR, the building's own return with no loan. The rest comes from borrowing at 5 percent against a property returning more than that. If the debt cost rose to 7 percent, the levered IRR would fall to about 13 percent while the risk to equity stayed the same, which is why I sized the loan to hold coverage above the covenant with rates two points higher.

title: Where Tax Leaks Out of a Return
summary: Tax leaks from a property return in five places: on the way in, during the hold, on distribution, at sale and through fees. Tax depreciation shelters income during the hold and is often recaptured on sale, and the character of the profit depends on facts. After-tax returns belong to each investor, not to the deal.
body:
A pre-tax return describes the property; an after-tax return describes your wealth. Between the two, money leaks at several points, and the size of the leak depends less on the building than on who owns it, how and where. Map the leaks before you compare deals.

Recall

Q. Last week's review covered stabilised NOI. What is the difference between potential gross income and effective gross income?

A. Potential gross income assumes every unit leased at market rent all year. Effective gross income subtracts vacancy and credit loss.

Q. In Week 13, LEX explained what happens when someone relies on your budget. When does a pro forma become a representation?

A. When you hand it to a lender or investor who relies on it; from then on, statements of fact in it can carry legal consequences.

Q. In Week 7, Omar explained the legal shape of your wealth. What does a personal guarantee do?

A. It makes you personally liable for a debt if the borrower does not pay, putting your own assets behind a project's loan.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Elias here. Investors and brokers quote returns before tax because that is the only number that is the same for everyone. Your number is different. Two investors in the same building, one taxed in one place and holding through a company, the other taxed elsewhere and holding personally, can end up with after-tax returns that differ by several percentage points. If you compare deals, or structure one, on pre-tax returns alone, you are comparing numbers neither of you will receive. I teach concepts here. I state no rate as fact, and every rule must be verified against the primary source and with a qualified adviser in each jurisdiction involved.

The five places tax leaks

In plain English, tax can be taken at five points between the building and your pocket.

  1. On the way in: transfer taxes, stamp duties or land registration charges when you buy, and value-added or goods and services tax on construction and some purchases. Week 23 maps these.
  2. During the hold: tax on the operating income, either at the level of the owning entity, at the level of the investor, or both.
  3. On the way out of the entity: tax on distributions, such as dividend tax or, when money crosses a border, withholding tax deducted at source.
  4. At sale: tax on the gain, and the recapture of earlier tax depreciation.
  5. Throughout: fees, which are not tax but leak in the same way, and which may themselves be taxable to the person who receives them.

The professional framing adds one question to each point: at which level is the tax charged, and can a tax paid at one level be credited at another? Some entities are taxed themselves; others are flow-through, meaning income passes through to the owners and is taxed only in their hands. Week 22 covers flow-through entities and residence; Week 58 covers repatriation and withholding.

Say that out loud now. In, during, out, at sale, and fees. Five places, and at each one ask who is taxed.

Depreciation shelters income now and is recaptured later

Many tax systems let an owner deduct tax depreciation on a building against its rental income. That deduction reduces tax during the hold without any cash leaving. But it also reduces the building's tax cost, so when the building is sold, some or all of the depreciation already deducted may be brought back into income. That is recapture. The details, which buildings qualify, at what rates and whether recapture is taxed as income or as a gain, vary widely and must be verified against the primary source.

First worked example, with hypothetical round numbers and a hypothetical tax rate of 25 percent chosen only to show the mechanics; it is not any jurisdiction's rate. A building distributes $400,000 of cash income in a year. Tax depreciation of $250,000 is available. Taxable income is $400,000 minus $250,000, which is $150,000. Tax at the hypothetical 25 percent is $37,500, leaving $362,500 after tax. Without the depreciation deduction, tax would have been $100,000, leaving $300,000. The deduction saved $62,500 this year. Over five years at the same figures, the building's tax cost has fallen by $1,250,000, and that is the amount exposed to recapture on sale.

At sale: recapture and the gain

Second worked example, continuing, with two hypothetical rates: 25 percent on recaptured depreciation and 15 percent on the remaining gain, again chosen only for illustration. The building cost $10,000,000 and you claimed $1,250,000 of tax depreciation, so its tax cost is now $8,750,000. You sell for $11,000,000, net of selling costs. The total taxable amount is $11,000,000 minus $8,750,000, which is $2,250,000. Of that, $1,250,000 is recapture and $1,000,000 is gain above original cost. Tax is $312,500 on the recapture plus $150,000 on the gain: $462,500. A pre-tax model that shows $1,000,000 of profit on sale has left out almost half a million dollars, and a pre-tax IRR has quietly assumed none of it was paid.

Notice the timing. Depreciation saved tax early and recapture charged it late. Even if the total tax were the same, the deferral has value, which is Nadia's time value of money from Week 11 working in your favour. That is why after-tax IRR, not just after-tax profit, is the comparison that matters.

Character: income or gain

Whether the profit on a project is treated as business income or as a capital gain can change its tax substantially, and it is decided on facts: why you acquired the property, how long you held it, what you did with it, and how you financed it. A developer who builds to sell is usually earning business income; an investor who holds for rent may be earning a gain on eventual sale. In Week 12 I noted that intention must be recorded at the time it is formed. Week 24 covers how tax authorities test substance over form.

After-tax returns are personal

Put it together. The pre-tax IRR of a deal is a property of the deal. The after-tax IRR is a property of the investor: their residence, their holding structure, whether they can use losses, and whether tax paid in one country is credited in another. When you present a deal, present the pre-tax returns as the deal's numbers, say plainly that they are before tax, and invite each investor to have their adviser model their own after-tax return. Never promise an after-tax figure to someone else.

Professional sign-off required: a qualified tax adviser in each jurisdiction where the property, the entity and each investor are taxed.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing between two deals, or two structures, on pre-tax returns when the after-tax difference is larger than the pre-tax difference. The control: for any deal you invest in yourself, ask your adviser for a one-page map of the five leak points and an after-tax IRR on your own holding structure before you commit.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats tax depreciation as free money. It is usually a deferral, and the bill can arrive at sale, sometimes when you have the least cash to pay it.

Callback

In Week 13, LEX warned that a budget handed to an investor becomes something they may rely on. So does a return. If your memo says "after-tax IRR of 12 percent" to an investor whose tax position you have not modelled, you have made a statement they may rely on and you cannot support. State pre-tax returns as the deal's, and leave after-tax figures to each investor's adviser.

Recap

Tax leaks in five places: on the way in, during the hold, on distribution, at sale and through fees. Tax depreciation shelters income during the hold and is often recaptured on sale. Character, income or gain, depends on facts and intention. After-tax returns belong to the investor, not the deal. Verify every rule against the primary source.

Next: Sage working a full return calculation, unlevered, levered and after tax, step by step.
checklist: Map the five leak points: in, during the hold, on distribution, at sale and fees.
Ask at each point whether the entity or the investor is taxed, and whether credits apply.
Track the tax cost of each building and the depreciation exposed to recapture.
Model tax at sale, not only tax during the hold.
Record your intention for each property at the time you acquire it.
Present pre-tax returns as the deal's and leave after-tax figures to each investor's adviser.
Verify every rate, rule and threshold against the primary source.
head: Field checklist
speak: A pre-tax return describes the property; an after-tax return describes my wealth. Tax leaks in five places: on the way in, through transfer and sales taxes; during the hold, on operating income; on the way out, through dividend or withholding tax; at sale, on the gain and the recapture of earlier depreciation; and through fees. At each one I ask who is taxed, the entity or the investor, and whether one tax is credited against another. Tax depreciation lowers tax during the hold but also lowers the building's tax cost, so some of it may be recaptured on sale; on a hypothetical example, a million dollars of profit on sale carried almost half a million of tax. Whether profit is income or gain depends on facts and intention. After-tax returns belong to each investor, so I present pre-tax returns as the deal's and leave after-tax figures to their advisers.
terms: Recapture — bringing previously deducted tax depreciation back into income when an asset is sold for more than its reduced tax cost.
Flow-through entity — an entity whose income is taxed in the hands of its owners rather than at the entity level.
Withholding tax — tax deducted at source by the payer, often when interest, dividends or fees are paid across a border.

hostile.q: Your memo shows a 14 percent IRR. What will I actually keep after tax?
hostile.a: I can't tell you that responsibly, because it depends on where you are taxed and how you hold your interest. The 14 percent is the deal's pre-tax return. The tax leaks are mapped on page three: transfer tax on the way in, income during the hold, distribution tax or withholding, recapture and gain at sale, and fees. Your adviser should model your after-tax return from that map before you commit.

title: One Deal, Three Returns: Unlevered, Levered and After Tax
summary: A worked calculation of one hypothetical deal three ways. The building earns an unlevered IRR of about 9.4 percent, a 60 percent loan at 5 percent lifts the equity IRR to about 15.8 percent, and illustrative tax brings it back to about 10.9 percent. IRR is found by hand by bracketing NPV between two rates.
body:
Work one deal three ways, unlevered, levered and after tax, and you will see exactly how much of a return comes from the building, how much from the loan, and how much never reaches you. You can find an IRR by hand by bracketing it between two discount rates.

Recall

Q. On Day 1, what does the equity multiple measure that IRR does not?

A. Size: how much cash came back relative to what went in, regardless of how long it took.

Q. In Week 13, Quincy built a budget from square metres. What did escalation after commitment do to the equity?

A. It ate the equity first: costs rose after the loan was fixed, so the shortfall had to be funded from the owner's money.

Q. In Week 7, Nadia calculated the concentration ratio. What does it measure?

A. The share of your net worth tied up in a single asset or project.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Sage here. Odd weeks we calculate forward. Today you will build the four return measures from one set of cash flows, by hand, in units, so that when a sponsor sends you a 16 percent IRR you can find out in five minutes whether the building earns it or the loan does, and what tax will take. All figures are hypothetical, and the tax figures are illustrations, not any jurisdiction's rules.

Step 1: The deal

You acquire a stabilised building for $10,000,000 today, year 0. It earns NOI of $700,000 in year 1 and $700,000 in year 2. You sell it at the end of year 2 for $10,500,000, net of selling costs. To keep the arithmetic visible, cash flows arrive at year end and there are no capital expenditures.

Step 2: Unlevered cash flows and returns

Without a loan: year 0, minus $10,000,000. Year 1, plus $700,000. Year 2, plus $700,000 of NOI plus $10,500,000 of sale proceeds, which is $11,200,000. Total cash back is $11,900,000. Unlevered equity multiple is $11,900,000 divided by $10,000,000, which is 1.19 times. Dollar profit is $1,900,000. Year 1 cash-on-cash is $700,000 divided by $10,000,000, 7 percent.

Now the IRR, by bracketing. Recall that IRR is the rate at which NPV is zero. Try 9 percent. Discount factors are 0.9174 for year 1 and 0.8417 for year 2. Present value is $700,000 times 0.9174, about $642,000, plus $11,200,000 times 0.8417, about $9,427,000: total about $10,069,000. Less the $10,000,000 invested, NPV is about plus $69,000. Try 10 percent. Factors 0.9091 and 0.8264. Present value is about $636,000 plus $9,256,000, about $9,893,000. NPV is about minus $107,000. NPV crossed zero between 9 and 10 percent. Interpolate: 9 plus 69 divided by 176, about 9.4 percent. The unlevered IRR is about 9.4 percent. That is the building's own return.

Step 3: Add the loan

Borrow $6,000,000 interest-only at a hypothetical 5 percent, repaid from the sale. Interest is $300,000 a year. Equity invested is $4,000,000. Equity cash flows: year 0, minus $4,000,000. Year 1, $700,000 of NOI less $300,000 of interest, which is $400,000. Year 2, $400,000 plus sale proceeds of $10,500,000 less the $6,000,000 loan repayment, which is $4,900,000.

Levered measures: cash back $5,300,000. Equity multiple $5,300,000 divided by $4,000,000, 1.325 times. Dollar profit $1,300,000. Year 1 cash-on-cash $400,000 divided by $4,000,000, 10 percent. IRR: at 15 percent, factors 0.8696 and 0.7561, present value about $348,000 plus $3,705,000, about $4,053,000, NPV about plus $53,000. At 16 percent, factors 0.8621 and 0.7432, present value about $345,000 plus $3,641,000, about $3,986,000, NPV about minus $14,000. Interpolate: about 15.8 percent.

Say that out loud now. The building earns about 9.4 percent. The loan lifts equity to about 15.8 percent. The dollar profit fell, from 1.9 million to 1.3 million.

That last point is worth a pause. Leverage raised the IRR and the multiple on equity, but total dollar profit fell by the $600,000 of interest paid. You earned a higher rate on less of your own money, which is the whole bargain of leverage, and the risk of losing that money rose with it, as Roman showed on Day 3.

Step 4: After tax

Elias's illustration, with hypothetical tax, not any jurisdiction's. Suppose your tax on the operating income is $60,000 each year, after depreciation deductions, and tax on the sale, including recapture, is $300,000. After-tax equity cash flows: year 0, minus $4,000,000. Year 1, $400,000 minus $60,000, which is $340,000. Year 2, $4,900,000 minus $60,000 minus $300,000, which is $4,540,000.

After-tax measures: cash back $4,880,000, multiple 1.22 times, profit $880,000. IRR: at 10 percent, present value about $309,000 plus $3,752,000, about $4,061,000, NPV about plus $61,000. At 11 percent, factors 0.9009 and 0.8116, present value about $306,000 plus $3,685,000, about $3,991,000, NPV about minus $9,000. Interpolate: about 10.9 percent.

Step 5: Read the four results together

MeasureUnleveredLeveredLevered, after tax
IRRabout 9.4%about 15.8%about 10.9%
Equity multiple1.19x1.33x1.22x
Dollar profit$1,900,000$1,300,000$880,000
Year 1 cash-on-cash7%10%8.5%

Leverage added about 6.4 points of IRR. In this illustration, tax took about 4.9 points back. A sponsor quoting "15.8 percent" is quoting a real number that you, as an investor in this hypothetical, would not experience.

Step 6: Ask what is at risk, and for how long

Returns tell you what you earn if the plan holds. Two more numbers tell you what you can lose if it does not. Peak equity is the most of your money in the deal at any one time; here it is $4,000,000 levered, from day one until the sale. Break-even sale price is the price at which equity gets its money back and no more. Levered, equity receives $800,000 of income over two years, so it needs $3,200,000 from the sale after repaying the $6,000,000 loan: a sale price of $9,200,000, about 12 percent below the $10,500,000 plan. Unlevered, the break-even sale price is $8,600,000, about 18 percent below plan. The loan raised the IRR from about 9.4 to about 15.8 percent, and it also cut the margin for error on the exit from about 18 percent to about 12. Put those two facts on the same page whenever you present the levered return.

Second worked example: more expensive debt

Same deal, but the loan costs 7 percent: $420,000 a year. Levered equity flows: minus $4,000,000; year 1, $700,000 minus $420,000, which is $280,000. Year 2, $280,000 plus $4,500,000, which is $4,780,000. Check the units every time; an error here is the commonest mistake in return models. Multiple: $5,060,000 divided by $4,000,000, about 1.27 times. Bracket the IRR: at 12 percent the NPV is about plus $60,000, and at 13 percent about minus $9,000, so the IRR is about 12.9 percent. Two points on the debt cost took about three points off the equity IRR, while the risk to equity stayed the same.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is accepting a model's IRR without rebuilding its cash flows, because a single misplaced loan repayment, a missing sale cost or a pre-tax figure labelled after-tax can move the answer by several points. The control: rebuild the equity cash flows yourself in a few lines, bracket the IRR between two rates, and compare it with the model.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner forgets to subtract the loan repayment from the sale proceeds in the levered case, and reports a spectacular IRR. The second mistake is to discount levered equity cash flows and then compare them with an unlevered hurdle.

Callback

In Week 11, Nadia taught NPV by hand. Today's IRR bracketing is the same arithmetic turned around: instead of choosing a rate and finding the NPV, you search for the rate that makes the NPV zero. If you can do one, you can do the other, and you never need to trust a spreadsheet blindly.

Recap

Lay out unlevered, levered and after-tax cash flows. Calculate multiple, profit and cash-on-cash directly. Find IRR by trying two rates whose NPVs straddle zero and interpolating. Read the four measures together: the building's return, what the loan adds, and what tax takes away.

Next: JAX, in the room with an investor who says your IRR is too good to be true.
checklist: Lay out unlevered, levered and after-tax equity cash flows by year.
Subtract the loan repayment from sale proceeds in the levered case.
Calculate equity multiple, dollar profit and cash-on-cash directly.
Bracket the IRR between two rates whose NPVs straddle zero, then interpolate.
Compare levered returns only with levered hurdles.
Show what the loan adds and what tax takes away.
Rebuild any sponsor's equity cash flows before trusting the model's IRR.
head: Field checklist
speak: I work one deal three ways. A 10 million dollar building earns 700,000 dollars a year and sells after two years for 10.5 million. Unlevered, the cash flows are minus 10 million, plus 700,000 and plus 11.2 million: a 1.19 times multiple, 1.9 million of profit and an IRR of about 9.4 percent, found by trying 9 and 10 percent and interpolating. With a 6 million loan at 5 percent, equity puts in 4 million and gets 400,000 and then 4.9 million back: 1.33 times, 1.3 million of profit, about 15.8 percent IRR. Leverage raised the rate and lowered the dollar profit. With illustrative tax, the equity IRR falls to about 10.9 percent. And if the loan costs 7 percent instead of 5, the levered IRR falls to about 12.9 percent. So I always ask how much is the building, how much is the loan and how much is tax.
terms: Bracketing — finding an IRR by hand by choosing two discount rates whose NPVs fall either side of zero.
Interpolation — estimating the IRR between two bracketing rates in proportion to how far each NPV is from zero.
Levered cash flow — the cash to equity after debt service and loan repayment.

hostile.q: Your model says 15.8 percent. My analyst gets 12. Who is right?
hostile.a: Let's rebuild the equity cash flows together; it takes five minutes. Equity in 4 million, 400,000 in year one after interest, and 4.9 million in year two after repaying the 6 million loan from a 10.5 million sale. At 15 percent the NPV is about plus 53,000 and at 16 percent about minus 14,000, so roughly 15.8. If your analyst is at 12, I'd check the interest rate: at 7 percent the same deal gives about 12.9. Either way, the unlevered return is about 9.4, and that is the building's own number.

title: The Investor Who Says Your IRR Is Too Good
summary: A scene with an experienced co-investor who challenges an 18 percent projected IRR. The lesson gives the lines to say and never to say, the question behind the question, when to stay silent and how to hold your state, and works through her counter-proposal on the promote hurdle.
body:
When an experienced investor says your IRR looks too good, she is not asking you to defend the number. She is asking whether you understand what produces it. Answer with the building's own return, what the loan adds, what could go wrong, and how you are paid.

Recall

Q. On Day 2, what was Rule 15?

A. I never accept an IRR without its equity multiple, dollar profit, hold period and after-tax figure beside it, and I never take a distribution that leaves the project unable to survive its downside case.

Q. In Week 13, Priya put you in front of a credit officer reviewing your budget. What was the safest answer to a number you did not have?

A. Say you will confirm it by a specific date, and then do, rather than guessing in the room.

Q. In Week 7, Roman ran the guarantee meeting. What is the lender really asking when it requests your personal financial statement?

A. Whether you could actually pay if the guarantee were called, and how much of your wealth is liquid rather than tied up in other projects.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, JAX here. Sophisticated equity partners have seen hundreds of pro formas, and almost all of them show attractive IRRs. What separates the sponsors they back from the ones they decline is not the headline return. It is whether the sponsor can take the return apart in front of them, calmly, and show where it could break. This scene is a hypothetical meeting with an existing co-investment partner reviewing a new project. How you may approach new investors is regulated, and Week 70 covers it; nothing here is a script for raising money.

The scene

Hypothetical. You are presenting a $10,000,000 development to a partner who invested with you before. Your summary shows a levered IRR of 18 percent. She reads it, puts the page down and says: "Eighteen percent on a development. Everyone shows me eighteen. Convince me this one is real."

The question behind the question

She wants four things. How much of the 18 is the property and how much is the loan? What happens to the return when something goes wrong, because something will? Does your compensation reward you for building value, or for making the IRR look good, for example by refinancing early? And will you tell her the bad version without being asked?

The lines to say

Start by agreeing with the premise: "You're right to push on it. Eighteen on its own tells you very little, so here is what's underneath it."

Then the decomposition: "The project's unlevered IRR is about 11 percent; that is the building's own return. The loan, at about 60 percent of cost, takes equity to 18. The equity multiple is 1.6 times over about three and a half years, which is $2,400,000 of profit on $4,000,000 of equity. All of that is before tax; your adviser should run your own after-tax figure."

Say that out loud now. Unlevered first, then what the loan adds, then the multiple and the hold, then the tax caveat.

Then the downside, before she asks: "If construction runs six months late and costs come in 5 percent over, the levered IRR falls to about 9 percent and the multiple to about 1.25. If the exit cap rate is half a point higher on top of that, equity roughly gets its money back. Here is the page."

Then your pay: "My promote starts above an 8 percent preferred return and requires a 1.4 times multiple as well, and it is paid on realised cash after sale or a refinance sized to our downside case. I can't earn it by taking your money back early."

The lines never to say

  • "That's conservative." Every sponsor says it. Show the downside instead.
  • "The IRR is after tax." Not unless you have modelled her tax, which you cannot.
  • "We'll refinance at stabilisation and get your capital back." Not without the coverage test at higher rates; Day 2's composite started exactly there.
  • "Trust me, I've done this before." She will judge the work, not the reassurance.

When to stay silent

After you show the downside page, stop and let her read it. A sponsor who keeps talking while an investor reads the bad case sounds as though he is trying to talk over it. If she asks a question you cannot answer exactly, say so: "I'll confirm that by Friday," and do.

Worked example: her counter

Hypothetical. She says: "I'll come in, but I want the promote hurdle at a 1.5 times multiple, not 1.4." Work it before answering. On the base case, the multiple is 1.6, so the promote is still earned, but on less of the profit. On the delay case, at about 1.25, neither hurdle is met either way. The change matters only in a middling outcome, say a 1.45 times result, where your promote disappears. Ask yourself whether a middling result reflects your management or the market. If you believe your downside is real, the higher hurdle is a fair price for her money and you might accept it in exchange for something you value, such as a faster decision or a commitment to the next project. That is Week 66's negotiation lesson applied to returns: trade on interests, not positions.

Holding your state

Being challenged on your own numbers can feel like being called a liar. It is not; it is her job. Hear "convince me" as "teach me," and slow down. Practitioner habit: before the meeting, say the decomposition aloud three times, so the first sentence comes out steady. Breathing drills belong in the car park with the engine off, never while driving. If stress affects your health, check that with your doctor.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk in this room is defending the headline number instead of explaining it, which tells an experienced investor that you either do not understand your return or do not want her to. The control is a one-page return summary that leads with unlevered IRR, shows what leverage adds, gives multiple, profit and hold period, includes a downside case, states that returns are pre-tax, and sets out how you are paid.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner hears scepticism and raises the return, finding an assumption to make the number look better. The professional lowers his voice and shows the downside.

Callback

In Week 6 you learned acknowledge, bridge, answer. It fits this scene exactly. Acknowledge: "You're right to push on it." Bridge: "Here is what's underneath it." Answer: unlevered return, leverage, multiple, downside, pay. The structure keeps you from arguing with a fair question.

Recap

When an investor challenges your IRR, agree it needs explaining, then decompose it: unlevered return, what leverage adds, multiple and hold period, a downside case offered before she asks, a pre-tax caveat, and a promote she can see does not reward early cash-outs. Stay silent while she reads the bad case.

Next: Kema's week 15 review, with six questions, a Red Pen drill and a boardroom drill.
checklist: Lead with the unlevered IRR, then show what the loan adds.
Give equity multiple, dollar profit and hold period beside every IRR.
Offer the downside case before the investor asks for it.
State that all returns are pre-tax and that her adviser should model her own.
Explain how your promote is earned and that it does not reward early cash-outs.
Stay silent while the investor reads the downside page.
Work any counter-proposal through base, middling and downside outcomes before answering.
head: Field checklist
speak: When a seasoned investor says my 18 percent IRR looks too good, I agree it needs explaining and then I take it apart. The building's own return, unlevered, is about 11 percent. The loan, at about 60 percent of cost, takes equity to 18. The multiple is 1.6 times over three and a half years, 2.4 million of profit on 4 million of equity, all before tax. Then I show the downside before she asks: six months late and 5 percent over budget, the IRR falls to about 9 and the multiple to about 1.25. Then my pay: the promote needs an 8 percent preferred return and a 1.4 times multiple, and it is paid on realised cash, so I cannot earn it by returning her money early. I never call my numbers conservative, never call a return after tax, and I stay silent while she reads the bad case.
terms: Preferred return — the return investors receive before the developer shares in profit, often called the pref.
Hurdle — a return threshold, such as an IRR or a multiple, that must be met before a promote is paid.
Return decomposition — breaking a levered return into the property's own return, what leverage adds, and what tax and fees remove.

hostile.q: If the project is late and over budget, do you still get paid?
hostile.a: I still earn the development fee for the work, at the rate in our agreement, but not the promote. In the delay case on page two the multiple is about 1.25, below the 1.4 hurdle, so I share in no profit above your return of capital and preferred return. That is deliberate: I want my upside tied to the same outcome as yours.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 15 Review: Returns, Leverage and the Red Pen
summary: Six questions on IRR versus multiple, the IRR traps, Rule 15, leverage, tax leakage and finding an IRR by hand; a recap of the week; a Red Pen drill on a flawed deal summary; and a two-minute boardroom explanation with a model answer.
body:
This week reduced to one habit: never read a return alone. IRR measures speed, the multiple measures size, cash-on-cash measures income, leverage changes all three, and tax decides what you keep. Today you test it, mark up a flawed deal summary, and explain returns to a board in two minutes.

Recall

Q. On Day 3, when is leverage positive?

A. When the property earns more than the debt costs, so borrowing raises the return on equity. When the debt costs more, leverage is negative.

Q. Week 13's review covered contingency and estimate classes. Why must every estimate carry its class?

A. Because the class tells the reader how accurate the number can be; an early estimate presented without it becomes a budget that cannot be met.

Q. Week 7's review covered wealth mindset under pressure. What does Rule 7 say?

A. Never let one project, or one lender's change of mind, be able to take everything; size every commitment so its worst case leaves your liquidity floor untouched.

Why this matters

Kema here. Mr Shabazz, returns are the language in which every investor and partner will judge you, and the language in which brokers will try to sell to you. A review is where you stop recognising the measures and start using them together, quickly, under pressure.

The six questions

Question 1. Deal A turns $100 into $200 over ten years; Deal B turns $100 into $130 over two years. Which has the higher IRR, and which the higher multiple? Answer: B has the higher IRR, about 14 percent against about 7.2. A has the higher multiple, 2.0 times against 1.3.

Question 2. Name the four IRR traps. Answer: Short holds, early distributions, the reinvestment assumption and scale.

Question 3. What does Rule 15 say? Answer: I never accept an IRR without its equity multiple, dollar profit, hold period and after-tax figure beside it, and I never take a distribution that leaves the project unable to survive its downside case.

Question 4. A $10,000,000 building earns $600,000. With a $6,000,000 loan at 7 percent interest-only, what is cash-on-cash, and is leverage positive? Answer: Interest is $420,000, cash to equity $180,000 on $4,000,000, which is 4.5 percent. Leverage is negative on cash yield, because the debt costs more than the 6 percent the building earns.

Question 5. Name the five places tax leaks from a return. Answer: On the way in, during the hold, on distribution, at sale including recapture, and through fees.

Question 6. How do you find an IRR by hand? Answer: Try two discount rates whose NPVs fall either side of zero, then interpolate between them in proportion to each NPV's distance from zero.

Say that out loud now. Speed, size, income, leverage, tax. Never one alone.

Recap of the week

Sage and Elias set out IRR, multiple and cash-on-cash, levered and unlevered, the four IRR traps and after-tax leakage. Ford and Roman took apart a composite case where an early refinance made the IRR and broke the project. Roman showed leverage as positive or negative, magnifying gains and losses alike. Elias mapped the five leak points and recapture. Sage worked one deal three ways and found the IRR by bracketing. JAX put you in front of a partner who said your IRR was too good.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical deal summary. It has seven planted defects. Find them before reading on.

Project Alpha. Projected IRR 24 percent, comfortably above our 12 percent unlevered target. Equity $4,000,000, loan $6,000,000. Sale in year 2 for $10,500,000; equity receives the full $10,500,000 plus income. Cash-on-cash 4 percent, calculated as cash to equity over total project cost. After-tax IRR 18 percent for all investors. Sponsor promote payable on achieving a 15 percent IRR, including on a refinance at stabilisation. Exit cap rate assumed half a point below today's.

The defects. One: the IRR is quoted without a multiple, a dollar profit or an explicit hold period. Two: a levered IRR is compared with an unlevered target. Three: sale proceeds are credited in full to equity without repaying the $6,000,000 loan, which inflates every return. Four: cash-on-cash is divided by total project cost instead of equity. Five: one after-tax IRR is claimed for all investors, though after-tax returns depend on each investor's own position. Six: the promote is on IRR alone and payable on a refinance, which rewards early cash-outs, the Day 2 pattern. Seven: the exit cap rate is assumed lower than today's, which flatters the sale price; a careful model assumes it higher.

Boardroom drill

Explain this week in two minutes to a board that understands business but not real estate returns. Then compare with this model answer.

"We judge every deal on four measures together. The internal rate of return tells us how fast our money grows. The equity multiple tells us how much it grows. Cash-on-cash tells us what we receive each year along the way. And we always look first at the unlevered return, which is what the building earns with no loan, before we look at what borrowing adds. Borrowing helps only while the building earns more than the debt costs, and it magnifies losses exactly as it magnifies gains. Every number we show you is before tax; tax can take several points off, and how much depends on how each of us holds the investment. We do not take money out early if it leaves the project unable to survive a bad case, and our partners' promotes require both a return and a multiple, so nobody is paid for speed alone."

The biggest risk

The biggest risk after this week is fluency with the formulas and blindness to the inputs: a correct IRR calculated on sale proceeds that were never reduced by the loan. The control is to rebuild the equity cash flows yourself, in a few lines, every time.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner picks the deal with the highest IRR. The professional asks for the unlevered return, the multiple, the downside and the tax, and then decides.

Callback

In Week 11, Rule 11 said a reported profit that does not turn into cash on schedule is a question I ask in writing. Returns carry the same discipline: an IRR built on cash that the plan assumes but has not yet received is a forecast, not a result. Ask when each dollar arrives, and what it depends on.

Recap

Speed, size and income are three different questions, answered by IRR, multiple and cash-on-cash. Leverage changes all three and the risk. Tax leaks in five places. Bracket an IRR by hand. Never take a distribution that breaks the downside.

head: The six questions
speak: This week I learned never to read a return alone. The IRR measures how fast money grows, the equity multiple how much, and cash-on-cash what I receive each year. Each can be unlevered, the building's own return, or levered, after the loan. Leverage helps only while the building earns more than the debt costs, and it magnifies losses as much as gains. The traps are short holds, early distributions, the reinvestment assumption and scale. Tax leaks on the way in, during the hold, on distribution, at sale with recapture, and through fees, and after-tax returns belong to each investor. I can find an IRR by hand by bracketing it between two rates. The composite case showed an early refinance making the IRR and breaking the project. So my rule is: no IRR without its multiple, profit, hold period and after-tax figure, and no distribution that breaks the downside.
terms: Hold period — the time between investing and receiving the final return, which every IRR must state.
Peak equity — the largest amount of equity at risk in a deal at any one time.
Break-even sale price — the sale price at which equity recovers exactly what it invested, after the loan is repaid.

hostile.q: Your deal summary only shows the IRR. Why should I read any further?
hostile.a: You shouldn't have to ask, and I've corrected it. The summary now shows unlevered and levered IRR, the equity multiple, dollar profit, hold period, peak equity, a downside case and a note that every figure is pre-tax. If any of those undermines the IRR, you will see it on the first page, not the last.
